How many people here ignore the fact that this video was made before the msrp announcement? (Which NV themselves raised right before the reveal)

The tech review business is tough and if you don't make a video on it ASAP, you will loose mindshare versus others (GN, LTT, HU have all stated the very short timespan they have to benchmark some cards before the Review NDA lifts at some times, and this likely was one of them)

Either way, now that GPUs have returned to earth in prices (aside Lovelace), the 3080Ti's value has increased massively, pretty much  invalidating the 4080-12GB (3080Tis can be found for 900$ new easily ATM) unless you *really* want Frame Generation or a few % better performance in pure path tracing workloads.

Although the sort of problem here is NV sort of put their Ampere stack in a corner in the high end with the 3080-12GB (A sku that was Shadow dropped over the later parts of the scalpocaypse after the 3080Ti came out), pretty much being the 3080 Super in disguise giving you the 3080Ti's memory bandwidth and a minor uptick in core counts versus the 3080-10GB.

text:
Even if the card was sold at msrp, it's 500$ for roughly and optimistically 15% more gaming performance to 3080. 
You are paying 500$ extra on top of 3080 for performance that is not noticeable in gaming session unless you're just watching fps counter. 
This much money buys you flagship CPU, if you don't have it already, you are likely to see same performance increase. 
It's much smarter over all to max out your CPU before going 3080TI or 3090, and in truth there's no reason to buy those cards anyway. So little gain.
Spend your money on something else cool, or bunch of things... it's 500$. 

If we lived in normal times, 3080 would be already a little cheaper, and if sli was a thing you'd be asking yourself, do I get 15% performance or nearly double for roughly the same cost.
SLI is no longer a thing for that reason, who'd in their right mind would like to fork out 500$ more to get 15% gain? when sli offered so much more performance. 
For a work station use, two 3080's would literally smash 3090 to bits, at 100$ cheaper MSRP.
SLI is dead because it makes halo products not sell, because anyone knows they don't offer any realistic value beside bragging rights.

text:
Nvidia changed the msrp from 1000$ to 1200$ immediately prior to release, reviewers were under the impression it was going to be $1000.

Either way, people need to stop whining about price, GPU's have been selling, a lot, at over double their MSRP, complain about scalpers all you want, but manufacturers have raised their prices significantly, and they're still getting scooped up and resold at huge markups, meaning MSRP is nowhere close to fair for these cards. Does it suck? Fuck yes, but that's literally how the market works, it's supply and demand. Demand exceeds supply, significantly, therefore the ONLY solution to the disparity is to raise the price to find equilibrium. 1200$ for the 3080ti sounds absurd, but if you look at the market, it's being scalped for significantly lower markup than the rest of the lineup, meaning it is not selling at as high of a markup, MEANING the 1200$ price is far, far closer to "correct" for the market conditions, than the 3080, and 3090.

text:
@BrandonWestfall  It depends on how you define a “good product” and it all comes down to price elasticity in the end. Graphics card are not perfectly inelastic, so “it can be as expensive as it can be and people who want it will buy it anyway” doesn’t make sense. There is a tipping point even for high-end gamers, beyond which it is no longer a good deal.
The thing is scalpers probably have a lower elasticity than high-end gamers as well, so gamers end up having to pay more than *they could have paid* for the same product. It’s not a good product for them b/c more gamers will be over the tipping point - do remember only a very small amount of buyers are truly completely insensitive to price.
For NV it’s a no brainer b/c at the time cards are two step next to being inelastic, so they jack up the price out of proportion when compared to past gen 80-Ti cards. To them it is a good product as it’s free dollars earned - at the cost of real gamers.
Read up on basic microeconomics before you educate others on “good products”. Unless you speak for NV which I doubt you do.

​ @quantumm3282  Regardless of gaming or workstation  purposes? As you stated that you don't even know what machine learning purposes are, it is no wonder you can't see any performance difference compared to 3080. I'm just wondering why do you bother to comment when you clearly not know. Machine learning tasks require a lot of computational power, and not all computational powers are the same. Cuda cores and tensor cores are some of the things that makes training a model ( which is a very time consuming part of machine learning) a whole lot easier. That is why 3090 is an amazing piece of hardware for someone like me who train models at home. 
Now 3090 is a very expensive card. But compared to 3080 Ti, it doesn't offer much more to justify its price difference. There are certainly use cases for that massive amount of Vram, but not everyone needs that. So I say again, for the right purpose, 3080 Ti is a very good bargine. 
I already seen the specsheet, did you? 3090 have almost 3 percent more cuda cores than 3080 Ti. While 3080 Ti has 17 percent more cuda cores than 3080. It is the same for tensorcores. So yeah, it is a reasonable MSRP for people who needs it. If you are a gamer, then it is a stupid thing to buy when there is a perfectly amazing card with better price.

text: @KingOfGorillas While Mac's Apple Silicon performance can be great in terms of efficiency, currently, and may be great in terms of sheer performance, after all ARM-based designs are powering some of the best Super Computers of the world, with the M1 successors (until Apple starts to introduce hardware fixes for improved process/thread security and caches/memory manipulations that could impact/nerf the new chip designs a bit) you might be getting 3060 or better performance... but you'd still need devs on board to get the ARM-optimised MacOS releases - and that's an issue, partly due to much of the gaming code heavily based on CISC X86 ISA MMX/SSE extension subsets to do respective work efficiently - replacing some of the multimedia extensions with comparative Apple/ARM solutions such as Neon is one thing, but then there still are many SIMD extensions on the X86 side that would require thorough recoding for ARM's available SIMD subsets, similarly many of the new games (eg. COD, Overwatch, Assassin's Creed or even Path of Exile as a free example) are actually using AVX family of extensions of X86 to provide performance expected of them by the consumers/players and since these have currently no direct drop-in replacements in Apple's ARM ISA of M1s, it makes direct ports to M1 (and possible successors) far more difficult and costly process to make it profitable to even entertain the idea from the companies' finanacial point of view... And in some cases, AVX instruction attempts on M1 simply crash the app/game. Heck, I believe I've seen PoE devs officially stating that they're not releasing M1-optimised binaries due to the fact that they've spent a lot of time to code for some AVX-specific/AVX-centric instructions and are heavily reliant on these vector extensions, and any ports would require a nearly complete rewrite/overhaul of the codebase, and that's not a viable option. Same possibly goes for several other dev teams out there... And that's just the CPU side, the GPU encumberance and reliance on Windows- or Microsoft-oriented API standards (DirectX etc.) entails further rework of the visual aspects to instead base on Metal/OpenGL/OpenCL etc. for better support and performance on Mac, or more broadly Unix, hardware. Perhaps if Apple went with larger/stronger SVE similar to the one used in Fugaku's A64FX chip but possibly even better suited to desktop oriented drop-in replacements with their own extra SVE/SVE2-like secret sauce "baked-in", the translation from X86's AVX to ARM's SVE could have been easier and more efficient to warrant devs attention to focus on Apple Silicon Macs, maybe some future designs targeted at Mac Pro will incorporate these... For the moment however, games with active development that do not focus on those specific X86 or Windows instruction sets and extensions can and might be ported, older as in really old titles without active support may work through emulation due to their lower hardware requirements, but newer titles that have gone very far into the rabbit hole of respective X86 PC-centric instructions/extensions/APIs to perform great may not see a full recode for the possible tiny market share due to profitability reasons and their emulation may just fail... And that's only when talking about Mac oriented sub-selection of games or Wine translation layers, I'm not even touching complex projects with devs focusing on either PCs or PS4/5 or Xbox. All of this means M1 Macs are not a good solution for gaming... unless you're into arcade-style simple projects or cloud gaming with subscription fees for limited titles availability and remote gaming experience drawbacks ;)

text: @KingOfGorillas Yeah exactly that's the issue... extra work that at most may net you less than 8% of the computers market (as per recent bloomberg reports, Macs account for under 8% of PCs sold 2020-2021... M1s are only part of that market, and in some cases those who bought them aren't the target demographic- as such any dev team, given the choice to get more features into Windows or Console releases that could net you more players/potential customers or build nearly from the ground up a release for M1 Mac users of whom only part would even be interested playing, would focus on the money-making platform first. Sure, M1 adds performance for the power envelope but it's still way less than a typical current gen Windows desktop platform and thus is not addressed as easily on meetings with financial departments etc. ;) And yeah, there's a selection of games, but many are just simple arcade ones, you know things closer to Tetris than to Thief, and even when those are in the app store they are X86 ones with M1/ARM ports not exactly fully working or bugproof ;) Yeah, it's still the beginning of a transition, maybe if Apple coordinated with Microsoft to get more devs into the ARM desktop market, whether Win10X/Win10onARM or MacOS, we could see more work actually done. Regardless, you still need to remember that even though there are and have been open standards or standards that eg. fare better for more diverse platform spectrum, like consoles, Windows PCs and unix/linux PCs, devs are still deeply in the MS DirextX or Windows APIs with many engines built for the 3 platforms with highest chance of gaining player base - 2 consoles and a Windows desktop PC, otherwise the games are more of a point'n'click/touch bus stop arcade style ones for android/ios...  So it's both reusal of current code bases that do not target Mac and M1, and the cost to extend those code bases to incorporate ARM desktops that limit any gaming potential from the developper and customer point of view. We'll see what the future holds in due time... And as to AVX requirements, I guess it all boils down to devs finally managing to master these compute intensive extensions for their products for eg. game logic/physics/ai or map generation, which possibly entailed training/dev/proofofconcept/extra work and expenses to get there in the first place, with M1 ARM now requiring to kind of rethink from the ground up big projects for currently little probable profit.
author: @marcin_karwinski

text:
@KingOfGorillas Well it seems we agree on many things, most of which is the fact that MacOS, as well as linux, still remains very much neglected despite both APIs and platforms mature enough and performant enough. In case of M1 Macs it's compounded due to MacOS and its APIs combined with by-design-limited/reduced ARM64 architecture and extensions. Of course the reason for such neglect stems from current code bases that would require extra work to recode/replatform properly, or even to begin work using more open or widely supported standards instead of copy-pasting/basing on previous projects... and that entails extra work to be done and consequently extra costs to explain to CEOs/CFOs etc.
By the way, I'm also a linux user and gamer, and I've tried game dev a bit, so yeah, I understand this.
And just for your information AVX is not that non-present you may think, it is after all on the market since 2008. It's just another specific extension to the SSE family that's been extended several gens now since late 90s... and in CPUs since 2011 SandyBridge and Bulldozer. Still, this extension family already spanning 3 "gens" has not been adopted in desktop software development as widely as Intel wants it to be but it's very useful for many compute intensive applications... The domain of HPC or servers, trickled down to consumer general purpose CPUs, nets you several benefits through the SIMD instructions or wide instruction-repurposeful registers. PoE AFAIK uses these to easier and faster generate maps and "coordinate" spawned monsters. Other game dev teams also apply these extensions to improve procedurally generated content/world creation... If they decided to go with M1 ARM recode/rebase they could utilise both the existing SVEs of the ARM architecture and maybe utilise all the "neural" cores or whatever they're called for improved AI or programmed content. But that's a lot of work someone needs to do first to show others it's worth it, and most businesses tend to play safe and go cheap for "guaranteed" profit ;) One needs a force of market disruptors to open the doors for others to follow through as well, and for consumers to entice companies. So maybe future Mac ARM will get more dev studios on its side...
Still there's one more area M1 and future gens need to address to further entice regular users to "jump" ship - Apple needs to get the hardware accelerated media de-/encoding complexes support more codecs, form H264 through H265 through VP9 through AV1, and do it efficiently with quality ouputs that either beat or equal nvidia's Ampere NVENC/NVDEC or Intel's latest QSV. That would further the pro-sumer aspirations of their platform...
But back to 3080Ti and its pro-sumer aspirations, similarly to future M1 successors, the manufacturer needs to open its SR-IOV capabilities beyond their current grid practices. Heck, they could make the 3090 even more enticing if they added in the driver itself switches to firmware for an easy partitioning of all of those cores and VRAM. That could get it far ahead of 3080Ti in terms of usability, but I guess nvidia won't do it. Same as Apple probably won't in their future SoCs that could potentially be managed through SR-IOV into multiple virtual M1s ;)
author: @marcin_karwinski

text: @KingOfGorillas Well without actually having a Windows only machine or MacOS on a day-to-day basis and instead using linux as my main OS without any issues for nigh on 2 decades, I'd say - to each their own ;) Apple certainly has the funds or corporate leverage to entice more AAA or most recent and sought after titles' dev teams/studios but they seem to focus on keeping their premium brand image intact and as with every corpo to keep the investors happy... Maybe if or once they decide to release a handheld or console alternative with a bitten apple logo, we'll see them pushing for more gaming. Now however they're  rolling big guns in courts against game platform which may impact other platforms willingness to go Mac... you know, corporate image, corporate policy and corporate politics influence environment targeting. Well, i'm not thinking strictly server type SR-IOV, I'm more inclined towards them possibly allowing in future products the partitioning of those leaked wishful thinking multicore setups which could just as well become dev platforms for any Mac  gaming development with the option to partition high performance gear into virtual base devices. That'd certainly help... Of course any price drops are just as welcome for any dev teams to prepare for, build against and test on multiple cheaper alternatives, but it's Apple... Virtualisation with paritioning could be even better for hardware accelerated VMs and/or containers thus possibly allowing simultaneous builds/tests on various "hardware" and software using a single build server. Even regular consumers could benefit more if Apple added virtualisation with partitioning to carve out part of the SoC for eg. side-loading Windows with hardware acceleration for the cases when neither Wine nor Mac allows an app you need to run and Windows VM is the only way to go. As to hardware accelerated stream transcoding facilities ina hardware - it's not only the software or API side, it's also HW optimisation and HW silicon complexes implementation - current M1 acceleration is impressive in terms of speed, but from what I've seen it's worse in produced quality (maybe deblocking algorithm thresholds implementation or color processing) without bitrate reductions - every HW implementation entails some drawbacks and this is their 1st foray into desktop/laptop CPU+GPU since their codevelopment with IBM of Power ISA, but competition from the blue team offer better quality with reduced bitrates at good speeds, the red's also speedy now with even good quality but failing at keeping bitrates low-enough, while green's are stradling the performance, quality and size between QSV and VCE. That's one of the areas Apple could easily score even more prosumer creator customers ;)  Nvidia at least also has their fairly cheap Jetson SBCs for the tinkerers and people wanting to learn how to better utilise their graphics technologies, but Apple's cheapest desktop/computer is Mini, otherwise devs can only play with iPad for some tablet and desktop targeted projects, neither is cheap or good enough for dev/build farms... Apple now should at least prepare their HW to be supported by AMD's FSR as that could further gaming capabilities of the platform. Nvidia uses its ecosystem of features pretty well to target both sccientific and gamery client types to differentiate and boost its sales against competition. Radeon group is now playing catch-up with a one gen worth of delay. Intel will soon join them with their QSV as a very important aspect as well as server-originated SR-IOV features as marketing-friendly benefits. And Apple with their prosumer target clientele who are often image or video processing focused seems to only play catch-up to the Windows PC platforms...

text: Honestly, I think everyone is REALLY overreacting. I think the only misfires here were that they CLEARLY scripted and shot the entire video in confidence that it was going to be $999 MSRP, and they probably should have added an addendum talking more about the price after the MSRP was revealed. It honestly does sound like they were convinced $999 would be the case. That's a misstep to be sure, and I'm sure he'll talk about that on Wan Show. If it were $999, however, everything he said would have been valid. The overall message of the video clearly isn't "3080 Ti > 3080", it's "3080 Ti > 3080". Compared to the 3090, it would have been a compelling option, buy-it-now for the PREMIUM end of the market, had it actually been $999. And honestly, the more I think about it, it was a fair assumption, because it was really was the most logical MSRP for Nvidia to hit, since they were (and are) not competing at that specific price point. Really, the only mistake was not delaying the video by a few hours to add an addendum to video. It really is bizarre how hostile everyone is being about this.

text: I see what you are saying, but I don't think LTT made this video with average gamers in mind, though, nor should they have, tbh. It's a premium, flagship card, that was always going to be priced into a market segment (and a buyer demographic) that is much more forgiving of diminishing returns. I honestly don't know how people aren't seeing it in that context. A lineup where the cheapest card is $650 in the best case scenario was never going to properly reflect bang for the buck or the average gaming. He never recommends it over a 3080, but he whole-heartedly recommends it over a 3090. Now, the part where I DO think LTT misstepped was in not adding an addendum to the video discussing the $1,199 MSRP, when they clearly wrote and shot the whole video expecting it to be $999 (which I honestly think was a fair assumption to make.) At $999 I think his whole argument would be valid, in the context of the 3080 ti being a premium card, and a 3090 alternative rather than a 3080 alternative. They just should have addressed the incorrect assumption mire directly.

text:
From what I've seen in reviews the card gets almost exclusively compared to the 3090 with good relative performance. But when seeing the gaming benchmarks comparing the 3080 with the Ti I see absolutely no argument that can be made to justify the MSRP (and much less so the inevitable market prices we'll be seeing), with most fps performance deltas being in the low ~10s or even single digits. A MSRP hike from $700 to $1200 for those barely perceptible performance gains is ludicrous and unjustifiable for any prospective customer that doesn't sit on a veritable mountain of disposable income to be able to afford such a poor financial decision.

I am honestly disappointed how the value proposition is being glossed over by so many otherwise reputable reviewers. No doubt part of Nvidia's marketing strategy to hold back on the MSRP until after most big tech websites/channels have gotten their reviews out to farm the clicks and I'm sure Nvidia has put out strict reviewing guidelines to compare the Ti to the 3090 rather than the 3080 as that seems to be the trend in every review I've seen with barely anyone at all mentioning the 3080 by name outside of the benchmark graph. That or you guys are bending over backwards trying to kiss Nvidia's chocolate star out of fear of getting scratched off the review sample recipient list.

To reiterate: disappointing.

author: @spearman792

text:
Most the people mining etherium with these cards are able to run their rigs from countries with cheaper electricity. It’s hardly worth doing from North America due to our power costs.

A lot of them will feel more incentivized to do it now because of the outrageous prices of GPU’s, so they feel as though once their rigs are no longer profitable that they can sell their mining GPU’s at a higher cost. The problem with that though is it’s a big risk. The new video card market could spike back up once there are more chips and completely crash for used cards and they will lose all of their investment and literally come out negative from their mining rigs.

Profiting from etherium mining generally requires being able to resell your initial investment (GPU’s etc). Or you’re coming out in the red.

Unless you’re able to get very good electricity cost in your country, it usually is just more worth buying it directly and simply investing. A lot of these suckers getting into mining actually lose money in the long term because they think it’s so easy and don’t pay attention to operational costs and initial investment.

text:
@dumbdiveer  No offense, but I don't understand how your post relates to the content in mine. For my personal system, the 3080ti is the card to get-- I want as many CUDA cores as possible for rendering, while 12GB VRAM matches the other cards in my system. A 3090 would be marginally "better", but only if every other card in the system also had 24GB VRAM, otherwise, it will default to whatever the lowest card is running (currently 12GB). Meanwhile, a 3080 would drag down the max VRAM of every other card to 10GB (since you can't exceed the value of the lowest VRAM card) and have fewer CUDA cores...that's not worth it, to me. I'd have to further reduce textures or other complexity, which creates more work (time), than the synergy a ti offers.

For the bulk of pure gamers, the 3080ti is not the best value, but the video explains how we got here. By all means, if you want to stick it to NVIDIA to prove a point, more power to you. For me? I have a load of other considerations.
author: @knroo-j1487
@Prodigyscenez

text:
​ @Prodigyscenez  I've already explained why a 3090 wouldn't be any more useful to me, for the simple fact that it's main differentiator is limited by other 12GB cards in my system-- the floor for purchasing one will always be higher than any other 30 series card, and it only scales upward from there, rendering your point moot. Your argument is also contingent on the idea, that because a 3080ti is a better fit for me, that I'd pay any price to get it-- how did you arrive at this assumption? As an actual statement of fact, I won't pay "way over MSRP", because like everyone else, I'm: 1. forced to deal with the primary barrier to entry, which is the shortage of ALL cards and 2. I will patiently wait for an opportunity, as I've continued to do until this point, instead of dumping cash on scalpers.

I'm also not concerned with speculating on why the 3080ti exists-- at the end of the day, it does, whether we like it or not. However, much like every other 30 series card right now, scarcity is by far the tallest issue, and so wishing any particular card away, wouldn't change anything. Literally, other actors in the market have every incentive to pay over MSRP, because the cards have become a passive money-making device, and so they can and will leverage this, taking the upfront hit for any card they can get, including the previous 20 series. It's a very unfortunate case of hyper-demand, where gamers and those who aren't making significant returns on investment, are in a worse position to compete for a limited pool of product, spanning across generations of cards. As such, there's no real case to be made, that if the 3080ti didn't exist, that it would magically alleviate the issue I've just outlined, or even make a hairs worth of difference in the scarcity of 30 series cards. In other words, if supply wasn't an issue and you could readily buy your preferred card of choice, you wouldn't care that  3080ti exists-- you'd just choose what works for you and/or go on with your business.

Someone else brought up Quadros, not me.

I work with 3d rendering and I use my 3080 with vray gpu renderign whenever possible and I have to say, ,on scenes with some complex objects, even a detailed rug with dense displacement, you wont be able to render with only 12gb VRAM. 

I have to go for cpu rendering and use my 64gb of ram even for some, not most, interior scenes, otherwise it crashes for lack of VRAM. Well thats also because VRAY does not have proper out of core rendering which also uses system RAM, but that would also slow things down some mind you.

So yeah, those 3d gpu benchmarks are just a simple test that do not truly represent the difference between these cards. Twice the VRAM is VERY important for gpu rendering.

If you were considering a 3090, then the 3080ti could be  "better value proposition"

if you were shopping for a 3080, then you know it's not that far behind so validates that decision....

If you're not in one of these groups, the debate is largely academic anyway....

After many unsuccessful trouble shooting attempts, new 1050w PSU and many software fixes, I came across information regarding HotSpot temps and how it should be only 10-15c about the GPU temp under load. So I installed GPU-Z and discovered that once I hit 60-65c on the GPU the HotSpot temperature starts to run away and crashes between 95-100c. I've had my card for about a year and half at this point and after many hours of gaming and rendering I'm afraid my card may have degraded which is why I'm only now starting to get these crashes. One solution I've seen for the HotSpot issue is to take the cooler off check to see if the thermal paste was applied evenly and then apply new thermal paste & reseat the cooler. I haven't attempted this as I don't want to risk voiding my warranty when I go to RMA my card. Right now my current bandaid is to cap the power at 60% in Precision X1. The GPU stays at around 45c and the HotSpot at around 70c and so far has not crashed after many long hours. Not sure if your black screen may be caused by something similar or not. Hope you find a solution!

author: @Noctiltua

text:
These are the things Linus did not tell you:

1 - The 3080 Ti is the first "80 Ti" series ever - I repeat, the first ever - to offer lower performance-per-dollar than its non-Ti counterpart.

2 - The 3080 Ti offers the smallest performance increase ever seen over its non-Ti counterpart. In big part, that's due to the fact that it is still based off the same GPU silicon (unlike the previous 3 generations, which all used a bigger and more powerful chip in the Ti variant).

3 - Despite the fact that the 3080 Ti offers the smallest performance increase over its non-Ti equivalent, it offers the biggest price increase ever seen in its class. From USD699 (non-Ti) to USD1199 (Ti), a USD500 increase that represents a +70% price uplift. As comparison, the previous "inflation champ", the 2080 Ti, MSRP'd at USD999, "only" USD300 (42%) above its non-Ti equivalents.

4 - This is the first time, ever, that Nvidia launches a single-GPU flagship at (well into) 4-digit values. And while the 2080 Ti FE did cost over USD1000, the MSRP for the non-FE (which was the vast majority of the market) was USD999, so the 2080 Ti was still a 3-digit MSRP product.

5 - With the price of the 3080 Ti, you can buy a 3080 AND a 3070 (that is, if you could find any of these cards). This is the first time, ever, that an 80 Ti card is so expensive that it allows you to buy both a 80-series and a 70-series of the same generation for its price. Even the highly expensive (and criticized) 2080 Ti was not expensive enough to allow you to buy both a 2080 and a 2070 for the same price.

6 - Scalpers are no excuse to increase the price of your products in such a disrespectful way. If anything, Nvidia's new pricing strategy just makes everything even worse. I'll explain with simple logic: it much worse to pay 2-3x MSRP over USD1,199 than it is to pay 2-3x MSRP over USD699.

7 - Because the RTX 3080 Ti is based off the same silicon as the RTX 3080 - you guessed it, 3080 production will have to be split with the 3080 Ti (not to mention the 3090, which also uses the same silicon). So if it was hard to get your hands on a 3080 previously, now it's going to become even harder. Thanks, Nvidia!

8 - Linus is the only big tech channel that is trying to sell you the 3080 Ti as something good, completely ignoring the fact that the 3080 launched last year already offered nearly the same performance for USD500 less (or, in scalper reality, ~USD1500 less). Good job in becoming an Nvidia sell-out, Linus!

I now have a 6900XT. I misclicked, while trying to get a 6800XT on AMDs website, but i am keeping it, because...well what should i buy instead?
I got EXTREMELY lucky with the 6900XT.
1000,- for a card is already too much, so the 1200,- are even more "too much". I am not happy with the 6900XT overall. It does not perform the way i hoped for, in the games i do play, it has the inferior featureset and on top of that, i lost the silicon-lottery, so this card REFUSES to be undervolted! The 16GB VRAM are worthless, since in resolutions it WOULD make a difference, Nvidia still pulls ahead!

BUT...given the current situation, i do not have a single alternative, so i guess i am stuck with a card i do not really want!
I KNOW...i know, i have a GPU and a new one, i know my bitching is the definition of a 1st world problem, but...

text:
Hi Linus tech tips
The Review is a little misleading about the VRAM,  

If you are using ARNOLD render (industry-standard unlike blender), or unreal real-time rendering with or without ray trace, and you have a large scene (unlike the common test scene), then you will feel the performance difference. it's easy to fill up 12 gigs of VRAM if you try to render heavy stuff. like fur, displacement, and hair with high quality, higher than a game. those things are BASIC for most projects that are considered to be "medium" quality nowadays. 

when an offline renderer like Arnold have no more VRAM left, it starts to fall back on the regular ram, and the cpu takes parts of the render. and that is slower ofc.  (talking about Arnold GPU / VRAY GPU mode)

if we are talking about unreal, it will start to downgrade the texture sizes in real-time, and ofc more VRAM means better FPS in ray trace. unreal fur + forest + 8K textures + real-time displacement + grass with dynamic shadows + ray trace and sh*t load of details is too much for a 12 gig ram card. 24VRAM gives you twice the distance of LOD-0 assets. 

Render artists can see this video and think "oh great ill just get the 3080ti then, no need for that ram". But if they are professionals, and creating renders of nature and characters in high quality, they most likely will need the 3090's ram.

text:
These are the things Linus did not tell you:

1 - The 3080 Ti is the first "80 Ti" series ever - I repeat, the first ever - to offer lower performance-per-dollar than its non-Ti counterpart.

2 - The 3080 Ti offers the smallest performance increase ever seen over its non-Ti counterpart. In big part, that's due to the fact that it is still based off the same GPU silicon (unlike the previous 3 generations, which all used a bigger and more powerful chip in the Ti variant).

3 - Despite the fact that the 3080 Ti offers the smallest performance increase over its non-Ti equivalent, it offers the biggest price increase ever seen in its class. From USD699 (non-Ti) to USD1199 (Ti), a USD500 increase that represents a +70% price uplift. As comparison, the previous "inflation champ", the 2080 Ti, MSRP'd at USD999, "only" USD300 (42%) above its non-Ti equivalents.

4 - This is the first time, ever, that Nvidia launches a single-GPU flagship at (well into) 4-digit values. And while the 2080 Ti FE did cost over USD1000, the MSRP for the non-FE (which was the vast majority of the market) was USD999, so the 2080 Ti was still a 3-digit MSRP product.

5 - With the price of the 3080 Ti, you can buy a 3080 AND a 3070 (that is, if you could find any of these cards). This is the first time, ever, that an 80 Ti card is so expensive that it allows you to buy both a 80-series and a 70-series of the same generation for its price. Even the highly expensive (and criticized) 2080 Ti was not expensive enough to allow you to buy both a 2080 and a 2070 for the same price.

6 - Scalpers are no excuse to increase the price of your products in such a disrespectful way. If anything, Nvidia's new pricing strategy just makes everything even worse. I'll explain with simple logic: it much worse to pay 2-3x MSRP over USD1,199 than it is to pay 2-3x MSRP over USD699.

7 - Because the RTX 3080 Ti is based off the same silicon as the RTX 3080 - you guessed it, 3080 production will have to be split with the 3080 Ti (not to mention the 3090, which also uses the same silicon). So if it was hard to get your hands on a 3080 previously, now it's going to become even harder. Thanks, Nvidia!

8 - Linus is the only big tech channel that is trying to sell you the 3080 Ti as something good, completely ignoring the fact that the 3080 launched last year already offered nearly the same performance for USD500 less (or, in scalper reality, ~USD1500 less). Good job in becoming an Nvidia sell-out, Linus!

author: @ObeyThePapaya

text:
@ObeyThePapaya  Well, you are correct in the way you describe it; price is determined by demand, and the true meaning of "overpriced" is that the price is so high no one will pay it. In that the RTX 3090 are not overpriced, because every one of them that gets made, gets sold, for a couple thousand dollars or even more.

However, there is meaning in discussing relative value, and the relative value can be viewed through the lens of what else there is and what it is valued at (as well as what came before). The prices, as set by Nvidia and the board partners, can be related to each other, considering their relative usefulness of the products for their intended tasks. In that, if the value of the RTX 3080 is $800, and it gives a certain level of performance, it is reasonable to compare its cost and performance ratio to the RTX 3080Ti at $1200 and say the 3080Ti is "overpriced" relative to the 3080 because its price/performance doesn't come anywhere near the price/performance ratio of the 3080. Or, more accurately still, "the price/performance ratio of the RTX 3080Ti compares unfavorably with the price/performance ratio of the RTX 3080 at the MSRP of each product". 

The way I said it fits within the common way of speaking most of us have, and we understand the limitations of being less than perfectly precise in our wording (or maybe I'm just projecting my ability to understand such things onto "most of us"), and take the meaning with its limitations in accuracy for what was intended. That said, thank you for pointing out my rather sloppy way of giving my opinions on this issue; I'll strive to do better in the future. 

Oh, and, it is a severe error to make assumptions without evidence, and you did that when you assumed I couldn't afford the RTX 3080Ti or 3090, or to pay scalper prices for one of those products. I have to wonder - why would you do that? Why would you even mention it at all, as it was not germane?😉

text:
These are the things Linus did not tell you:

1 - The 3080 Ti is the first "80 Ti" series ever - I repeat, the first ever - to offer lower performance-per-dollar than its non-Ti counterpart.

2 - The 3080 Ti offers the smallest performance increase ever seen over its non-Ti counterpart. In big part, that's due to the fact that it is still based off the same GPU silicon (unlike the previous 3 generations, which all used a bigger and more powerful chip in the Ti variant).

3 - Despite the fact that the 3080 Ti offers the smallest performance increase over its non-Ti equivalent, it offers the biggest price increase ever seen in its class. From USD699 (non-Ti) to USD1199 (Ti), a USD500 increase that represents a +70% price uplift. As comparison, the previous "inflation champ", the 2080 Ti, MSRP'd at USD999, "only" USD300 (42%) above its non-Ti equivalents.

4 - This is the first time, ever, that Nvidia launches a single-GPU flagship at (well into) 4-digit values. And while the 2080 Ti FE did cost over USD1000, the MSRP for the non-FE (which was the vast majority of the market) was USD999, so the 2080 Ti was still a 3-digit MSRP product.

5 - With the price of the 3080 Ti, you can buy a 3080 AND a 3070 (that is, if you could find any of these cards). This is the first time, ever, that an 80 Ti card is so expensive that it allows you to buy both a 80-series and a 70-series of the same generation for its price. Even the highly expensive (and criticized) 2080 Ti was not expensive enough to allow you to buy both a 2080 and a 2070 for the same price.

6 - Scalpers are no excuse to increase the price of your products in such a disrespectful way. If anything, Nvidia's new pricing strategy just makes everything even worse. I'll explain with simple logic: it much worse to pay 2-3x MSRP over USD1,199 than it is to pay 2-3x MSRP over USD699.

7 - Because the RTX 3080 Ti is based off the same silicon as the RTX 3080 - you guessed it, 3080 production will have to be split with the 3080 Ti (not to mention the 3090, which also uses the same silicon). So if it was hard to get your hands on a 3080 previously, now it's going to become even harder. Thanks, Nvidia!

8 - Linus is the only big tech channel that is trying to sell you the 3080 Ti as something good, completely ignoring the fact that the 3080 launched last year already offered nearly the same performance for USD500 less (or, in scalper reality, ~USD1500 less). Good job in becoming an Nvidia sell-out, Linus!

text:
I get that this was recorded ahead of launch, but this has got to be one of the worst reviews I've seen come out of this channel in a long time. There is literally NOTHING to be happy about with this launch,  and it's basically nothing but a cash grab. Allow me to explain a few points:

1.Since the RTX 3080Ti uses binned-down GA102 chips, these are chips that didn't meet the RTX 3090 spec. Without this card, these chips would've been made into the cheaper and better value RTX 3080. This card releasing means less RTX 3080 stock while more chips are diverted to this overpriced, terrible value card.

2. Literally, ANY CURRENT GEN CARD looks like good value compared to the 3090, so the point that the 3080Ti is cheaper and thus a better value is completely pointless. A better comparison would've been to more reasonably priced cards like the RTX 3080, RX 6800XT, or even the RX 6900XT.

3. Even against it's main competitor, the RX 6900XT (which in and of itself is a terrible value), The RTX 3080 Ti seems like utter garbage. Assuming MSRP (LOL), you're paying $200 for 4GB less VRAM, 6% slower performance in 1440p, and a measly 3% faster performance at 4K (numbers from Hardware Unboxed).

Overall, this cash-grab of a launch is in no way "a winner", and is deserving of much more than 2 seconds of a frowny face as a response.

text:
These are the things Linus did not tell you.

1 - The 3080 Ti is the first "80 Ti" series ever - I repeat, the first ever - to offer lower performance-per-dollar than its non-Ti counterpart.

2 - The 3080 Ti offers the smallest performance increase ever seen over its non-Ti counterpart. In big part, that's due to the fact that it is still based off the same GPU silicon (unlike the previous 3 generations, which all used a bigger and more powerful chip in the Ti variant).

3 - Despite the fact that the 3080 Ti offers the smallest performance increase over its non-Ti equivalent, it offers the biggest price increase ever seen in its class. From USD699 (non-Ti) to USD1199 (Ti), a USD500 increase that represents a +70% price uplift. As comparison, the previous "inflation champ", the 2080 Ti, MSRP'd at USD999, "only" USD300 (42%) above its non-Ti equivalents.

4 - This is the first time, ever, that Nvidia launches a single-GPU flagship at (well into) 4-digit values. And while the 2080 Ti FE did cost over USD1000, the MSRP for the non-FE (which was the vast majority of the market) was USD999, so the 2080 Ti was still a 3-digit MSRP product.

5 - With the price of the 3080 Ti, you can buy a 3080 AND a 3070 (that is, if you could find any of these cards). This is the first time, ever, that an 80 Ti card is so expensive that it allows you to buy both a 80-series and a 70-series of the same generation for its price. Even the highly expensive (and criticized) 2080 Ti was not expensive enough to allow you to buy both a 2080 and a 2070 for the same price.

6 - Scalpers are no excuse to increase the price of your products in such a disrespectful way. If anything, Nvidia's new pricing strategy just makes everything even worse. I'll explain with simple logic: it much worse to pay 2-3x MSRP over USD1,199 than it is to pay 2-3x MSRP over USD699.

7 - Because the RTX 3080 Ti is based off the same silicon as the RTX 3080 - you guessed it, 3080 production will have to be split with the 3080 Ti (not to mention the 3090, which also uses the same silicon). So if it was hard to get your hands on a 3080 previously, now it's going to become even harder. Thanks, Nvidia!

8 - Linus is the only big tech channel that is trying to sell you the 3080 Ti as something good, completely ignoring the fact that the 3080 launched last year already offered nearly the same performance for USD500 less (or, in scalper reality, ~USD1500 less). Good job in becoming an Nvidia sell-out, Linus!

text:
I wouldn't call it insane, but it should be obvious to anyone buying a card for that price that what they pay additionally is far more than what they get in terms of performance. That still doesn't necessarily make it a "bad" choice – more performance is still more performance, but it also doesn't make it the better choice.
I personally spent 850€ each on two GTX 1080s a few years ago and ended up regretting it with decreasing Sli support (although the setup rocked in Sli games, and never did terribly), but getting an RTX 3080 FTW3 in January for 985€, I am happy.
Now, I'm not particularly wealthy, and the CPU upgrade I need to fully utilize that 3080 has been pushed further and further, but I really, fundamentally enjoy having a high-end GPU. It isn't the experience of playing RTX games at Ultra settings, because let's be honest: The game doesn't become significantly worse at Medium graphics with RTX off – but the fact that I can do that is something I very much enjoy. Pushing benchmarks to the limits, running Minecraft with path tracing shaders – all this shit that nobody really needs is shit I love doing, and for that, it's worth it to me.
It's like buying a sports car. This is never a "reasonable" thing to do. Nobody needs a sports car, and for far less money, you can get cars that are far better suited for everyday tasks. This makes it a good decision to buy such a car. However, there are many people to whom it is worth it to spend that money to enjoy just owning that sports car or taking it on a race track, and I think it would be unfair to say they are "wrong" or insane.
The price has to match what you want from the thing you buy, not just in terms of performance, but how much you enjoy owning it. For most gamers, high-end GPUs don't do that because all they want is play games, understandably. But for some, they do.

It's so hard, being from a smaller city in Canada. I have literally never seen a single "in-stock" option for online since the launch of 3000 series. We're coming up to a year since launch. That quite honestly paints a picture of "there's been 0 allocated stock to Canadian retailers". Even though, Memory Express had "in-stock", it was "in-store" only, which as someone who lives almost 1000km from the closest Memory Express, let alone the almost 3000km from the store that had the stock, it's very disheartening. 

I hope this stuff gets better, not just for gaming, but I can't imagine what the Auto Industry is like right now. My parent's dealership had 0 vehicles to sell at one point because they just couldn't get a vehicle delivered. My dad's new F-150, a used car dealer offered 75k for it... the sticker price is 76k, that's unheard of!
